entries.name: The EnterpriseReady SaaS Feature Guides
entries.description: The majority of the features making B2B users happy will be implemented by the IAM perimeter.

entries.name: IAM is hard. It's really hard.
entries.description: “Overly permissive AWS IAM policies that allowed s3:GetObject to * (all) resources”, led to $80 million fine for Capital One. The only reason why you can't overlook IAM as a business owner.

entries.name: IAM Is The Real Cloud Lock-In
entries.description: A little click-baity, but author admit that “It depends on how much you trust them to 1. Stay in business; 2. Not jack up your prices; 3. Not deprecate services out from under you; 4. Provide more value to you in business acceleration than they take away in flexibility.”

entries.name: Enterprise Information Security
entries.description: Mozilla's security and access guidelines.

entries.name: Mitigating Cloud Vulnerabilities
entries.description: “This document divides cloud vulnerabilities into four classes (misconfiguration, poor access control, shared tenancy vulnerabilities, and supply chain vulnerabilities)”.

entries.name: Cartography
entries.description: 🆓 A Neo4J-based tool to map out dependencies and relationships between services and resources. Supports AWS, GCP, GSuite, Okta and GitHub.

entries.name: Open guide to AWS Security and IAM
As a user, I want…
entries.description: A meta-critic of account management, in which features expected by the business clash with real user needs, in the form of user stories written by a fictional project manager.

entries.name: Things end users care about but programmers don't
entries.description: In the same spirit as above, but broader: all the little things we overlook as developers but users really care about. In the top of that list lies account-centric features, diverse integration and import/export tools. I.e. all the enterprise customers needs to cover.

entries.name: Separate the account, user and login/auth details
entries.description: Sound advice to lay down the foundation of a future-proof IAM API.

entries.name: Identity Beyond Usernames
entries.description: On the concept of usernames as identifiers, and the complexities introduced when unicode characters meets uniqueness requirements.

entries.name: Kratos
entries.description: 💸 User login, user registration, 2FA and profile management.

entries.name: UserFrosting
entries.description: 🆓 Modern PHP user login and management framework.

entries.name: Cryptographic Right Answers
entries.description: An up to date set of recommendations for developers who are not cryptography engineers. There's even a shorter summary available.

entries.name: Real World Crypto Symposium
entries.description: Aims to bring together cryptography researchers with developers, focusing on uses in real-world environments such as the Internet, the cloud, and embedded devices.

entries.name: An Overview of Cryptography
entries.description: “This paper has two major purposes. The first is to define some of the terms and concepts behind basic cryptographic methods, and to offer a way to compare the myriad cryptographic schemes in use today. The second is to provide some real examples of cryptography in use today.”

entries.name: Papers we love: Cryptography
entries.description: Foundational papers of cryptography.

entries.name: Lifetimes of cryptographic hash functions
entries.description: “If you are using compare-by-hash to generate addresses for data that can be supplied by malicious users, you should have a plan to migrate to a new hash every few years”.

entries.name: Security Recommendations for Any Device that Depends on Randomly-Generated Numbers
entries.description: “The phrase 'random number generator' should be parsed as follows: It is a random generator of numbers. It is not a generator of random numbers.”

entries.name: RFC #4122: UUID - Security Considerations
entries.description: “Do not assume that UUIDs are hard to guess; they should not be used as security capabilities (identifiers whose mere possession grants access)”. UUIDs are designed to be unique, not to be random or unpredictable: do not use UUIDs as a secret.

entries.name: Awesome Identifiers
entries.description: A benchmark of all identifier formats.

entries.name: Awesome GUID
entries.description: Funny take on the global aspect of unique identifiers.

entries.name: BeyondCorp: A New Approach to Enterprise Security
entries.description: Quick overview of Google's Zero-trust Network initiative.

entries.name: What is BeyondCorp? What is Identity-Aware Proxy?
entries.description: More companies add extra layers of VPNs, firewalls, restrictions and constraints, resulting in a terrible experience and a slight security gain. There's a better way.

entries.name: oathkeeper
entries.description: 💸 Identity & Access Proxy and Access Control Decision API that authenticates, authorizes, and mutates incoming HTTP requests. Inspired by the BeyondCorp / Zero Trust white paper.

entries.name: Pomerium
entries.description: 💸 An identity-aware proxy that enables secure access to internal applications.

entries.name: heimdall
entries.description: 🆓 A cloud-native, identity-aware proxy and policy enforcement point that orchestrates authentication and authorization systems via versatile rules, supporting protocol-agnostic identity propagation.

entries.name: SPIFFE/SPIRE
entries.description: 🆓 A CNCF framework issuing short-lived, cryptographically-verifiable identities (SVIDs) to workloads across heterogeneous environments.

entries.name: NanoMDM
entries.description: 🆓 Minimalist Apple MDM server and library to enroll and manage the identity of Apple devices, inspired by MicroMDM.

entries.name: API Tokens: A Tedious Survey
entries.description: An overview and comparison of all token-based authentication schemes for end-user APIs.

entries.name: A Child's Garden of Inter-Service Authentication Schemes
entries.description: In the same spirit as above, but this time at the service level.

entries.name: Scaling backend authentication at Facebook
entries.description: How-to in a nutshell: 1. Small root of trust; 2. TLS isn't enough; 3. Certificate-based tokens; 4. Crypto Auth Tokens (CATs). See the slides for more details.

entries.name: The new NIST password guidance
entries.description: A summary of NIST Special Publication 800-63B covering new password complexity guidelines.

entries.name: Password Storage Cheat Sheet
entries.description: The only way to slow down offline attacks is by carefully choosing hash algorithms that are as resource intensive as possible.

entries.name: Password expiration is dead
entries.description: Recent scientific research calls into question the value of many long-standing password-security practices such as password expiration policies, and points instead to better alternatives such as enforcing banned-password lists and MFA.

entries.name: Practical Recommendations for Stronger, More Usable Passwords
entries.description: This study recommend the association of: blocklist checks against commonly leaked passwords, password policies without character-class requirements, minimum-strength policies.

entries.name: Banks, Arbitrary Password Restrictions and Why They Don't Matter
entries.description: “Arbitrary low limits on length and character composition are bad. They look bad, they lead to negative speculation about security posture and they break tools like password managers.”

entries.name: Dumb Password Rules
entries.description: 🆓 Shaming sites with dumb password rules.

entries.name: Password Manager Resources
entries.description: 🆓 A collection of password rules, change URLs and quirks by sites.

entries.name: A Well-Known URL for Changing Passwords
entries.description: 🆓 Specification defining site resource for password updates.

entries.name: How to change the hashing scheme of already hashed user's passwords
entries.description: Good news: you're not stuck with a legacy password saving scheme. Here is a trick to transparently upgrade to stronger hashing algorithm.

entries.name: Breaking Password Dependencies: Challenges in the Final Mile at Microsoft
entries.description: The primary source of account hacks is password spraying (on legacy auth like SMTP, IMAP, POP, etc.), second is replay attack. Takeaway: password are insecure, use and enforce MFA.

entries.name: Beyond Passwords: 2FA, U2F and Google Advanced Protection
entries.description: An excellent walk-trough over all these technologies.

entries.name: A Comparative Long-Term Study of Fallback Authentication
entries.description: Key take-away: “schemes based on email and SMS are more usable. Mechanisms based on designated trustees and personal knowledge questions, on the other hand, fall short, both in terms of convenience and efficiency.”

entries.name: Secrets, Lies, and Account Recovery: Lessons from the Use of Personal Knowledge Questions at Google
entries.description: “Our analysis confirms that secret questions generally offer a security level that is far lower than user-chosen passwords. (…) Surprisingly, we found that a significant cause of this insecurity is that users often don't answer truthfully. (…) On the usability side, we show that secret answers have surprisingly poor memorability”.

entries.name: How effective is basic account hygiene at preventing hijacking
entries.description: Google security team's data shows 2FA blocks 100% of automated bot hacks.

entries.name: Your Pa$$word doesn't matter
entries.description: Same conclusion as above from Microsoft: “Based on our studies, your account is more than 99.9% less likely to be compromised if you use MFA.”

entries.name: Attacking Google Authenticator
entries.description: Probably on the verge of paranoia, but might be a reason to rate limit 2FA validation attempts.

entries.name: Compromising online accounts by cracking voicemail systems
entries.description: Or why you should not rely on automated phone calls as a method to reach the user and reset passwords, 2FA or for any kind of verification. Not unlike SMS-based 2FA, it is currently insecure and can be compromised by the way of its weakest link: voicemail systems.

entries.name: Getting 2FA Right in 2019
entries.description: On the UX aspects of 2FA.

entries.name: 2FA is missing a key feature
entries.description: “When my 2FA code is entered incorrectly I'd like to know about it”.

entries.name: SMS Multifactor Authentication in Antarctica
entries.description: Doesn't work because there are no cellphone towers at stations in Antarctica.

entries.name: Authelia
entries.description: 🆓 Open-source authentication and authorization server providing two-factor authentication and single sign-on (SSO) for your applications via a web portal.

entries.name: Kanidm
entries.description: 🆓 Simple, secure and fast identity management platform.

entries.name: SMS 2FA auth is deprecated by NIST
entries.description: NIST has said that 2FA via SMS is bad and awful since 2016.

entries.name: SMS: The most popular and least secure 2FA method

entries.description: Definitive research project demonstrating successful attempts at SIM swapping.

entries.name: Hackers Hit Twitter C.E.O. Jack Dorsey in a 'SIM Swap.' You're at Risk, Too.

entries.name: Clearing up some misconceptions about Passkeys
entries.description: Or why passkeys are not worse than passwords.

entries.name: Webauthn and security keys
entries.description: Describe how authentication works with security keys, details the protocols, and how they articulates with WebAuthn. Key takeaway: “There is no way to create a U2F key with webauthn however. (…) So complete the transition to webauthn of your login process first, then transition registration.”

entries.name: Getting started with security keys
entries.description: A practical guide to stay safe online and prevent phishing with FIDO2, WebAuthn and security keys.

entries.name: OpenSK
entries.description: 🆓 Open-source implementation for security keys written in Rust that supports both FIDO U2F and FIDO2 standards.

entries.name: YubiKey Guide
entries.description: Guide to using YubiKey as a SmartCard for storing GPG encryption, signing and authentication keys, which can also be used for SSH. Many of the principles in this document are applicable to other smart card devices.

entries.name: PKI for busy people
entries.description: Quick overview of the important stuff.

entries.name: Everything you should know about certificates and PKI but are too afraid to ask
entries.description: PKI lets you define a system cryptographically. It's universal and vendor neutral.

entries.name: lemur
entries.description: 🆓 Acts as a broker between CAs and environments, providing a central portal for developers to issue TLS certificates with 'sane' defaults.

entries.name: CFSSL
entries.description: 🆓 A swiss army knife for PKI/TLS by CloudFlare. Command line tool and an HTTP API server for signing, verifying, and bundling TLS certificates.

entries.name: JA4+
entries.description: 💸 A suite of network fingerprinting methods to facilitate threat-hunting and analysis.

entries.name: Introduction to JSON Web Tokens

entries.name: Learn how to use JWT for Authentication
entries.description: Learn how to use JWT to secure your web app.

entries.name: Using JSON Web Tokens as API Keys
entries.description: Compared to API keys, JWTs offers granular security, homogeneous auth architecture, decentralized issuance, OAuth2 compliance, debuggability, expiration control, device management.

entries.name: Hardcoded secrets, unverified tokens, and other common JWT mistakes
entries.description: A good recap of all JWT pitfalls.

entries.name: Adding JSON Web Token API Keys to a DenyList
entries.description: On token invalidation.

entries.name: Stop using JWT for sessions
entries.description: And why your "solution" doesn't work, because stateless JWT tokens cannot be invalidated or updated. They will introduce either size issues or security issues depending on where you store them. Stateful JWT tokens are functionally the same as session cookies, but without the battle-tested and well-reviewed implementations or client support.

entries.name: JWT, JWS and JWE for Not So Dummies!
entries.description: A signed JWT is known as a JWS (JSON Web Signature). In fact a JWT does not exist itself — either it has to be a JWS or a JWE (JSON Web Encryption). Its like an abstract class — the JWS and JWE are the concrete implementations.

entries.name: JOSE is a Bad Standard That Everyone Should Avoid
entries.description: The standards are either completely broken or complex minefields hard to navigate.

entries.name: JWT.io
entries.description: Allows you to decode, verify and generate JWT.

entries.name: Why Authorization is Hard
entries.description: Because it needs multiple tradeoffs on Enforcement which is required in so many places, on Decision architecture to split business logic from authorization logic, and on Modeling to balance power and complexity.

entries.name: The never-ending product requirements of user authorization
entries.description: How a simple authorization model based on roles is not enough and gets complicated fast due to product packaging, data locality, enterprise organizations and compliance.

entries.name: RBAC like it was meant to be
entries.description: How we got from DAC (unix permissions, secret URL), to MAC (DRM, MFA, 2FA, SELinux), to RBAC. Details how the latter allows for better modeling of policies, ACLs, users and groups.

entries.name: The Case for Granular Permissions
entries.description: Discuss the limitations of RBAC and how ABAC (Attribute-Based Access Control) addresses them.

entries.name: In Search For a Perfect Access Control System
entries.description: The historical origins of authorization schemes. Hints at the future of sharing, trust and delegation between different teams and organizations.

entries.name: Semantic-based Automated Reasoning for AWS Access Policies using SMT

entries.name: Authorization Academy
entries.description: An in-depth, vendor-agnostic treatment of authorization that emphasizes mental models. This guide shows the reader how to think about their authorization needs in order to make good decisions about their authorization architecture and model.

entries.name: Athenz
entries.description: 🆓 Set of services and libraries supporting service authentication and role-based authorization for provisioning and configuration.

entries.name: Biscuit
entries.description: Merges concepts from cookies, JWTs, macaroons and Open Policy Agent. “It provide a logic language based on Datalog to write authorization policies. It can store data, like JWT, or small conditions like Macaroons, but it is also able to represent more complex rules like role-based access control, delegation, hierarchies.”

entries.name: Cerbos
entries.description: 💸 An authorization endpoint to write context-aware access control policies.

entries.name: FerrisKey
entries.description: 🆓 Self-hosted, open-source, RBAC system written in Rust.

entries.name: Keto

entries.name: Ladon

entries.name: Casbin

entries.name: Open Policy Agent
entries.description: 🆓 An open-source general-purpose decision engine to create and enforce ABAC policies.

entries.name: Zanzibar: Google's Consistent, Global Authorization System
entries.description: Scales to trillions of access control lists and millions of authorization requests per second to support services used by billions of people. It has maintained 95th-percentile latency of less than 10 milliseconds and availability of greater than 99.999% over 3 years of production use. Other bits not in the paper. Zanzibar Academy is a site dedicated to explaining how Zanzibar works.

entries.name: SpiceDB
entries.description: 💸 An open source database system for managing security-critical application permissions inspired by Zanzibar.

entries.name: Permify
entries.description: 💸 Another open-source authorization as a service inspired by Google Zanzibar, and see how it compares to other Zanzibar-inspired tools.

entries.name: Topaz
entries.description: 💸 An open-source project which combines the policy-as-code and decision logging of OPA with a Zanzibar-modeled directory.

entries.name: Open Policy Administration Layer
entries.description: 💸 Open Source administration layer for OPA, detecting changes to both policy and policy data in realtime and pushing live updates to OPA agents. OPAL brings open-policy up to the speed needed by live applications.

entries.name: An AWS IAM Security Tooling Reference

entries.name: Become an AWS IAM Policy Ninja

entries.name: Policy Sentry
entries.description: 🆓 Writing security-conscious IAM Policies by hand can be very tedious and inefficient. Policy Sentry helps users to create least-privilege policies in a matter of seconds.

entries.name: IAM Floyd
entries.description: 🆓 AWS IAM policy statement generator with fluent interface. Helps with creating type safe IAM policies and writing more restrictive/secure statements by offering conditions and ARN generation via IntelliSense. Available for Node.js, Python, .Net and Java.

entries.name: IAMbic
entries.description: 💸 GitOps for IAM. The Terraform of Cloud IAM. IAMbic is a multi-cloud identity and access management (IAM) control plane that centralizes and simplifies cloud access and permissions. It maintains an eventually consistent, human-readable, bi-directional representation of IAM in version control.

entries.name: Google's Macaroons in Five Minutes or Less
entries.description: If I'm given a Macaroon that authorizes me to perform some action(s) under certain restrictions, I can non-interactively build a second Macaroon with stricter restrictions that I can then give to you.

entries.name: Macaroons: Cookies with Contextual Caveats for Decentralized Authorization in the Cloud
entries.description: Google's original paper.

entries.description: As a consumer/verifier of macaroons, they allow you (through third-party caveats) to defer some authorization decisions to someone else. JWTs don't.

entries.name: Gubernator
entries.description: 🆓 High performance rate-limiting micro-service and library.

entries.name: Descope

entries.name: Awesome OpenID Connect

entries.name: An Illustrated Guide to OAuth and OpenID Connect

entries.name: OAuth in one picture
entries.description: A nice summary card.

entries.name: PKCE Explained

entries.name: Hydra

entries.name: Keycloak
entries.description: 🆓 Open-source Identity and Access Management. Supports OIDC, OAuth 2 and SAML 2, LDAP and AD directories, password policies.

entries.name: Casdoor
entries.description: 🆓 A UI-first centralized authentication / Single-Sign-On (SSO) platform based. Supports OIDC and OAuth 2, social logins, user management, 2FA based on Email and SMS.

entries.name: authentik
entries.description: 💸 Open-source Identity Provider similar to Keycloak.

entries.name: ZITADEL
entries.description: 💸 An Open-Source solution built with Go and Angular to manage all your systems, users and service accounts together with their roles and external identities. ZITADEL provides you with OIDC, OAuth 2.0, login & register flows, passwordless and MFA authentication. All this is built on top of eventsourcing in combination with CQRS to provide a great audit trail.

entries.name: obligator
entries.description: 🆓 Simple and opinionated OpenID Connect server designed for self-hosters. Single static binary with flat-file or SQLite storage.

entries.name: The Difference Between SAML 2.0 and OAuth 2.0
entries.description: “Even though SAML was actually designed to be widely applicable, its contemporary usage is typically shifted towards enterprise SSO scenarios. On the other hand, OAuth was designed for use with applications on the Internet, especially for delegated authorisation.”

entries.name: What's the Difference Between OAuth, OpenID Connect, and SAML?

entries.name: The Beer Drinker's Guide to SAML

entries.name: The Difficulties of SAML Single Logout

entries.name: You either die an MVP or live long enough to build content moderation

Humans are great in one of these dimensions: accuracy. The downside is that humans are expensive and slow. Machines, or robots, are great at the other two dimensions: cost and speed - they're much cheaper and faster. But the goal is to find a robot solution that is also sufficiently accurate for your needs.”
